subject: Business Models
title: The Franchise Disclosure Document
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Franchise Disclosure Document.

hook.text: Before you buy a franchise, US law requires a 100+ page disclosure document. Most people don't read it.

buildup.text: The FDD lists fees, litigation history, franchisee success rates, and financial obligations.

discovery.text: Item 19 shows actual earnings data. Shockingly, many franchisors choose not to disclose this—it's optional.

twist.text: Some FDDs reveal that 30-40% of franchisees close within 5 years. It's buried in the fine print.

climax.text: The FDD is your best protection as a buyer—but only if you read it carefully with a franchise attorney.

punchline.text: 100 pages of truth. Most franchisees sign without reading.

quiz.question: What does Item 19 of the FDD contain?

details.summary: The Franchise Disclosure Document is a legally mandated report that franchisors must provide to prospective franchisees at least 14 days before signing..
details.whyItMatters: The FDD is the most important document in any franchise investment decision. Item 19, the financial performance representation, reveals actual earnings data that separates promising opportunities from money pits..
takeaways: The FDD must be provided at least 14 days before any franchise agreement signing
23 sections cover everything from litigation history to financial performance
Item 19 contains optional but crucial financial performance data from existing units

faq.question: What are the most important sections of the FDD to review?
faq.answer: Item 3 covers litigation history against the franchisor. Item 7 details total initial investment ranges. Item 19 provides financial performance representations from existing locations. Item 20 shows franchisee turnover rates. These four sections reveal the most about franchise viability.

faq.question: Why do some franchisors not include Item 19 financial data?
faq.answer: Item 19 is optional. Some franchisors omit it because their financial results are poor, because they fear legal liability if actual results differ from representations, or because they want to control the financial narrative through verbal discussions rather than written commitments.
